# Different spacings, one coordinate map

[Predict the coordinates before you run the code.]{.lesson-deck}
:::

A rectangular grid need not have cubic cells. With an origin $o$ and
spacing $h$, the coordinate of index $(i,j,k)$ is

$$
\begin{gathered}
x=o_x+i h_x, \\
y=o_y+j h_y, \\
z=o_z+k h_z.
\end{gathered}
$$

OpenPFC keeps size, origin and spacing explicit, so an initial condition
can be written in physical coordinates even when the cells are anisotropic.

## Let the domain do the conversion

```{.cpp include="model.cpp" snippet="geometry" dedent=2}
```

For index $(3,2,1)$, the example obtains $(-0.25,3,13)$. Mapping those
coordinates back recovers the original index. The other probes exercise
the first and last stored points. `to_indices` rounds each component to
the nearest grid index; it is not a field interpolator.

## Distinguish a coordinate map from a boundary rule

```sh
openpfc run model.cpp input.json --launcher=none
```

Edit the constants in `model.cpp`; the empty input is unused. The program
prints a CSV table with both conversions. The regression checks all three
physical coordinates and every recovered index against the affine formula.

Try a point halfway between two samples, then a point outside the box.
The conversion does not clamp or wrap indices. Periodic wrapping belongs
to the operation that needs it. Similarly, changing $h_x$ must change an
x derivative's scale: a coordinate conversion alone does not implement
that derivative. The [heat comparison](../../heat/fourier/index.qmd) uses
physical wave numbers for this reason.

This refactors the former strong-types domain demonstration into one
coordinate experiment. The public
[domain header](https://github.com/VTT-ProperTune/OpenPFC/blob/master/include/openpfc/kernel/data/domain.hpp)
is the contract for rounding and endpoint conventions.

The complete [C++ model](model.cpp) and [starting input](input.json)
are available with this lesson.
